lesson.title: Give data a shape

lead.text: NumPy is the library that supplies this container, and by convention it is imported as np. Its array is a grid of values that all have the same type. A plan with 2 rows of 3 seats, each marked with a seat number, is np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]). The outer brackets hold the rows, and each inner pair of brackets is one row.

An array knows its own dimensions. Its shape lists the number of rows first and then the number of columns, so this plan has shape (2, 3). The attribute size counts every value, which is rows times columns, so here it is 6. Each entry in the shape belongs to one axis, which is a direction along which the grid extends. The attribute ndim counts the axes. A table has two. A hall with several floors needs three, and np.zeros((3, 2, 5)) builds a block of zeros with 3 floors of 2 rows of 5 seats, so its ndim is 3.
The shape is written as a pair of numbers. Read which position stands for the rows.

A list and an array answer to the same arithmetic in different ways. Multiply a list by 2 and Python repeats it: [2, 4, 6] * 2 is [2, 4, 6, 2, 4, 6], a list twice as long. Multiply an array by 2 and NumPy applies the 2 to every value, so np.array([2, 4, 6]) * 2 is [4, 8, 12], the same length as before. Because an array holds one type of value, NumPy can run the same operation over all of it at once, and no loop is needed. Step through both.

afterFigure.text: That is why arrays suit data work. A price rise, a unit conversion or a rescaling is one line applied to the whole grid. It also means the same operator can mean two things, depending on whether its left side is a list or an array, so check which one you hold before you read a multiplication.

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.array([2, 4, 6])
result = values * 2

lead.text: Multiplying an array scales every value. Work out the scaled values before you add them.

steps.headline: An array has shape (3, 4). How many elements and how many axes does it have?

workedSteps.text: Shape gives rows, then columns: 3 rows of 4 values. How many elements is that?
Each entry of the shape is one axis. How many axes does the array have?

steps.headline: The same seats laid out again

lead.text: The same twelve seats could be laid out as 3 rows of 4, 4 rows of 3 or 2 rows of 6. NumPy does this with reshape, which gives back the values in a new shape. np.arange(10) makes the numbers 0 to 9, and np.arange(10).reshape(2, 5) arranges them as 2 rows of 5. The values are read off in order and fill the new rows from the left, so the first row holds 0 to 4.

One rule governs every reshape: rows times columns must equal the size. Ten values fit 2 by 5, 5 by 2 and 1 by 10. They cannot fit 3 by 5, which needs fifteen, because reshape never invents a value to fill a gap and never drops one to make things fit. If the numbers disagree, NumPy stops with an error.
Compare the number of values with what the new shape would need.

steps.headline: What are the shape and size of np.arange(10).reshape(2, 5)?

lead.text: See how the shape and the size follow from one call.

workedSteps.text: arange(10) holds the ten values 0 to 9. reshape(2, 5) lays them out as rows of five.
size counts every element: rows times columns.

lead.text: Counting the rows or columns yourself gets tedious and is easy to get wrong. Give reshape a -1 for one dimension and NumPy works that dimension out for you. It divides the number of values by the dimensions you did give. For twelve values, reshape(3, -1) means 3 rows and as many columns as are needed, which is 12 ÷ 3 = 4. reshape(-1, 2) means 2 columns and as many rows as are needed, which is 12 ÷ 2 = 6. Only one dimension can be -1, because two unknowns could not be told apart. Step through both.

afterFigure.text: The first result has 3 rows of 4 and the second has 6 rows of 2. Both hold the same twelve numbers in the same order. If the division does not come out even, NumPy stops with an error, since a whole grid cannot be made.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12)
result = a.reshape(3, -1)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12)
result = a.reshape(-1, 2)

lead.text: The columns are fixed. Divide the number of values by the dimension you gave.

One more property follows from an array holding a single type. Each array has a dtype, its data type, such as int16 for a whole number stored in 16 bits or int64 for one stored in 64 bits. A bit is a single 0 or 1, and 8 bits make a byte. Every value in the array takes the same number of bytes, so int16 takes 2 bytes per value and int64 takes 8. The attribute itemsize reports it.

That makes the memory an array needs easy to work out: the number of values times the bytes per value. An int64 array of 50 values takes 400 bytes. A Python int has no such fixed width and grows as its value grows. The fixed width is part of why NumPy is fast, and it has a cost. Each dtype has a largest value it can hold, and a bigger number no longer fits.
Work out how many bytes one value takes, then scale up to all the values.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([12, 30], dtype=np.int16)
bytes_per_item = a.itemsize

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([12, 30], dtype=np.int64)
bytes_per_item = a.itemsize

lesson.orientation: Build NumPy arrays and track dimensions, shape and element counts.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A cinema has 5 rows with 6 seats in each, and every seat is the same kind. The booking system keeps a plan of the hall. Ask it for the number of seats and it multiplies 5 by 6. Ask it to raise every ticket price by 10 per cent and it makes the same change to each seat without anyone going through them one by one. Ask for the plan rearranged as 3 rows of 10 and it lays out the same seats again, with none gained or lost.

A Python list is a poor fit for that job. It can hold anything, so it keeps a note of what each item is. It has no idea that its items form a hall. Ages were fine in a list, but data work usually means thousands of values of one kind in a grid, and a better container exists for them.

This lesson meets that container. It starts with the plan itself and how to read its dimensions. Then it asks how a whole plan is calculated on at once and how the same seats can be laid out again. It ends with the memory each seat takes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read an array's shape, count its elements, and reshape it without losing or inventing a value.

recap.keyIdea: An array's shape lists rows then columns and its size is their product. reshape rearranges exactly that many values, and array dtypes have a fixed width.

blocks.text: You counted 30 seats in the cinema. You found that np.array([3, 5]) * 2 sums to 16, that an array of shape (3, 4) holds 12 elements across 2 axes, and that 18 values reshaped with a -1 into 3 rows make 6 columns.

recap.nextHook: The hall plan can be laid out any way you like, and a plan is only useful if you can calculate from it. The takings for each row, the figure for each column and a price change for just one row are all questions about the same grid. The next lesson shows how to calculate across the right axis.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of np.array([3, 5]) * 2?
hints: Scale each array element before adding.
Multiply every element, then add.
Work out 3 × 2 + 5 × 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Elementwise multiplication gives [6, 10], whose sum is 16.

questions.onCorrect: 16. Multiplying the array scaled each element to 6 and 10, and the sum added them.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the second scaled element. Every element is scaled, and then all of them are added.
That adds the two elements without scaling them.

questions.prompt: How many elements are in an array with shape (3, 4)?
hints: Multiply the dimension sizes.
There are three rows, each with four elements.
Work out 3 × 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 3 rows of 4 values, giving 12 elements.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Three rows of four values gives the size, rows times columns.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the dimensions. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: Can an array of ten values be reshaped to (3, 4)?
hints: Compare the size with the product of the dimensions.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A (3, 4) shape requires twelve elements. reshape does not add or remove values.

questions.onCorrect: No. A (3, 4) grid holds twelve values. reshape never adds or drops any.

misconceptions.feedback: reshape never invents values. It only rearranges what is there.
reshape never discards values. The counts must already match.

questions.prompt: An array of 100 values has dtype int16. How many bytes do its values take?
hints: How many bytes does one int16 value use?
int16 uses 16 bits and a byte is 8 bits.
Multiply the bytes per value by 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: int16 is 2 bytes per value, and 100 × 2 = 200.

questions.onCorrect: 200. Every int16 value takes 2 bytes, so 100 values take 200. A Python int has no fixed width like that.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts bits. The question asks for bytes, and a byte is 8 bits.
That is the number of values. Each takes more than one byte.

hints: The inferred dimension must keep all the elements.
The reshape retains eighteen elements.
Divide the total by the three rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Eighteen values divided among three rows gives six columns.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Eighteen values over three rows gives six columns.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts. Divide the total by the rows.
That is the number of rows you gave. The -1 is the column count.

questions.prompt: How many dimensions does np.zeros((2, 3, 4)) have?
hints: Count the axes, not their product.
Each entry in the shape describes one axis.
Count the entries in the tuple.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The shape has three axes, so ndim is 3. Its size is 24.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The shape has three entries, so there are three axes. Its size, 24, is a different number.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the entries and gives the size. ndim counts the axes.

hints: Is values a list or an array?
Multiplying a list repeats it.
Count the items after repeating three times.
questions.prompt: With values = [4, 5, 6] as a plain Python list, what is len(values * 3)?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The list is repeated three times, giving 9 items.

questions.onCorrect: 9. A list repeats under multiplication, so three items three times is nine. An array would scale instead.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the original length. Multiplying a list repeats its items.

hints: Each row has the same number of seats.
Multiply the rows by the seats in each row.
Work out 5 × 6.
questions.prompt: How many seats does the cinema have in total?
questions.onCorrect: 30. Rows times seats per row. An array's size is its rows times its columns in the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers. Each of the 5 rows has 6 seats, so multiply.

hints: Shape is written rows first, then columns.
questions.prompt: For an array with shape (2, 3), which number is the row count?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first entry of shape is the number of rows.

questions.onCorrect: The first number. Shape lists rows, then columns, so (2, 3) is 2 rows of 3.

misconceptions.feedback: The second number counts columns. Rows come first.
The product is size, the number of elements, not the rows.

hints: Which number did we give reshape first?
questions.prompt: Why is the shape (2, 5) and not (5, 2)?

choices.label: Shape lists the rows first, then the columns
The larger number always comes second

acceptedIdeas: Shape lists the rows first, then the columns
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first entry of shape is the number of rows.

questions.onCorrect: Shape lists the rows first, then the columns, in the order reshape was given.

misconceptions.feedback: Shape follows the order you gave. The size of a number does not matter.
reshape keeps the order you gave. It does not sort.

hints: Each entry of the shape belongs to one axis.
Count the entries in the shape (3, 4).
Do not multiply them.
questions.prompt: How many axes does the array have?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The shape (3, 4) has two entries, so ndim is 2.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The shape has two entries, so the array has two axes. ndim counts axes, not elements.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size, the number of elements. ndim counts the axes.

hints: The reshape must keep all twenty elements.
The columns are fixed at 4.
Divide the total by the columns.
questions.onCorrect: 5. Twenty values in rows of 4 make 5 rows, which is what -1 asks NumPy to work out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of columns you gave. The -1 is the row count.
That multiplies the two numbers. Divide the total by the columns.
